Invariance of the Kaup-Kupershmidt equation and triangular auto-Bäcklund transformations11 1 Communicated by F. Calogero

Marianna Euler and Norbert Euler

Department of Engineering Sciences and Mathematics
Luleå University of Technology
SE-971 87 Luleå, Sweden
Emails: marianna@ltu.se; norbert@ltu.se

Abstract: We report triangular auto-Bäcklund transformations for the solutions of a fifth-order evolution equation, which is a constraint for an invariance condition of the Kaup-Kupershmidt equation derived by E. G. Reyes in his paper titled “Nonlocal symmetries and the Kaup-Kupershmidt equation” [J. Math. Phys. 46, 073507, 19 pp., 2005]. These auto-Bäcklund transformations can then be applied to generate solutions of the Kaup-Kupershmidt equation. We show that triangular auto-Bäcklund transformations result from a systematic multipotentialisation of the Kupershmidt equation.

1 Introduction

In his paper [7], Reyes reports an invariance of the Kaup-Kupershmidt equation

qt=qx​x​x​x​x+5​q​qx​x​x+252​qx​qx​x+5​q2​qx,\displaystyle q_{t}=q_{xxxxx}+5qq_{xxx}+\frac{25}{2}q_{x}q_{xx}+5q^{2}q_{x}, (1.1)

by the following

Proposition 1: [7] The Kaup-Kupershmidt equation, (1.1), is invariant under the transformation q↦q¯q\mapsto\bar{q}, in which

q¯=q+3​(ln⁡B)x​x,\displaystyle\bar{q}=q+3\left(\ln B\right)_{xx}, (1.2)

where the variables qq and BB are related by

q⁡(x,t)=−Bx​x​xBx+34​(Bx​xBx)2\displaystyle q(x,t)=-\frac{B_{xxx}}{B_{x}}+\frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{B_{xx}}{B_{x}}\right)^{2} (1.3)

and B⁡(x,t)B(x,t) is a solution to

Bt=Bx​x​x​x​x−5​Bx​x​Bx​x​x​xBx−154​Bx​x​x2Bx+654​Bx​x​x​Bx​x2Bx2−13516​Bx​x4Bx3.\displaystyle B_{t}=B_{xxxxx}-5\frac{B_{xx}B_{xxxx}}{B_{x}}-\frac{15}{4}\frac{B_{xxx}^{2}}{B_{x}}+\frac{65}{4}\frac{B_{xxx}B_{xx}^{2}}{B_{x}^{2}}-\frac{135}{16}\frac{B_{xx}^{4}}{B_{x}^{3}}. (1.4)

In the current letter we report a class of auto-Bäcklund transformations, known as the triangular auto-Bäcklund transformations (or △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformations [5]), by a systematic multipotentialisation of the equation (1.4). Triangular auto-Bäcklund transformations have been defined and demonstrated in our recent paper [5]. For details on the multipotentialisation procedure we refer the reader to our papers [3] and [4]. We show that the equation,

vt=vx​x​x​x​x−5​vx​x​vx​x​x​xvx+5​vx​x2​vx​x​xvx2\displaystyle v_{t}=v_{xxxxx}-5\frac{v_{xx}v_{xxxx}}{v_{x}}+5\frac{v_{xx}^{2}v_{xxx}}{v_{x}^{2}} (1.5)

plays a central role in the construction of solutions of the Kaup-Kupershmidt equation and consequently we find the general stationary solution of (1.5) by calculating its first integrals.

We remark that both equations (1.4) and (1.5) first appeared in a paper by J. Weiss [9] on the Painlevé analysis in the form of singularity manifold constraints for the Kupershmidt equation (see eq. (3.32) in [9]) and the Caudrey-Dodd-Gibbon equation (see eq. (3.21) in [9]), respectively. For more details on the Painlevé analysis and singularity manifolds we refer the reader to [8]. Furthermore, both (1.4) and (1.5) are known symmetry-integrable equations and appear in [6] as part of the list of fifth-order semilinear integrable evolution equations (see equations (4.2.12) and (4.2.11) in [6]). The recursion operators for both equations (1.4) and (1.5) are given in [2].

2 Multipotentialisations and △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformations

Let

ut=F⁡[u]\displaystyle u_{t}=F[u] (2.1)

denote an evolution equation in uu, where F⁡[u]F[u] denotes a given function that depends in general on xx, tt, uu and xx-derivatives of uu. The procedure to potentialise (2.1) in the equation

vt=G⁡[vx]\displaystyle v_{t}=G[v_{x}] (2.2)

is well known (see e.g. [1] and [4]). Equation (2.2) is known as the potential equation of (2.1). For the benefit of the reader and to establish the notation we describe this procedure briefly: The potentialisation of (2.1) in (2.2), if it exists, is established by a conserved current Φt​[u]\Phi^{t}[u] of (2.1) and the relation to the potential variable vv is then

vx=Φt​[u],\displaystyle v_{x}=\Phi^{t}[u], (2.3)

where

Dt​Φt​[u]+Dx​Φx​[u]|ut=F⁡[u]=0\displaystyle\left.\vphantom{\frac{DA}{DB}}D_{t}\Phi^{t}[u]+D_{x}\Phi^{x}[u]\right|_{u_{t}=F[u]}=0 (2.4)

and Φx\Phi^{x} is the conserved flux of (2.1). Here DtD_{t} and DxD_{x} are the total tt- and xx-derivatives, repectively. Conserved currents, Φt​[u]\Phi^{t}[u], for (2.1) can be obtained by the relation

Λ⁡[u]=E^​[u]​Φt​[u],\displaystyle\Lambda[u]=\hat{E}[u]\Phi^{t}[u], (2.5)

where Λ\Lambda is an integrating factor (also called multiplier) of (2.1) that can be calculated by the relation

E^​[u]​(Λ⁡[u]​ut−Λ⁡[u]​F​[u])=0.\displaystyle\hat{E}[u]\left(\Lambda[u]u_{t}-\Lambda[u]F[u]\right)=0. (2.6)

Here E^​[u]\hat{E}[u] is the Euler operator,

E^​[u]=∂∂u−Dx∘∂∂ux−Dt∘∂∂ut+Dx2∘∂∂u2​x−Dx3∘∂∂u3​x+⋯.\displaystyle\hat{E}[u]=\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u}-D_{x}\circ\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u_{x}}-D_{t}\circ\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u_{t}}+D^{2}_{x}\circ\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u_{2x}}-D_{x}^{3}\circ\frac{\partial\ }{\partial u_{3x}}+\cdots.

A multipotentialisation of (2.1) exists if (2.2) can also be potentialised. A △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformation for (2.1) exists if (2.2) potentialises back into the original equation (2.1). In fact we have define three different types of △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformations. Details are in [5], where several examples of △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformations are given for some third-order and fifth-order evolution equations, as well as for systems in (1+1) dimensions and higher dimensional evolution equations.

Our starting point is the Kupershmidt equation

Kt=Kx​x​x​x​x+λ⁡(Kx​Kx​x​x+Kx​x2)−λ25​(K2​Kx​x​x+5​Kx​Kx​x+Kx3)+λ4125​K4​Kx\displaystyle K_{t}=K_{xxxxx}+\lambda\left(K_{x}K_{xxx}+K^{2}_{xx}\right)-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{5}\left(K^{2}K_{xxx}+5K_{x}K_{xx}+K_{x}^{3}\right)+\frac{\lambda^{4}}{125}K^{4}K_{x} (2.7)

which potentialises under

Ux=K\displaystyle U_{x}=K (2.8)

in the first potential Kupershmidt equation,

Ut=Ux​x​x​x​x+λ​Ux​x​Ux​x​x−λ25​(Ux2​Ux​x​x+Ux​Ux​x2)+(λ5)4​Ux5,\displaystyle U_{t}=U_{xxxxx}+\lambda U_{xx}U_{xxx}-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{5}\left(U_{x}^{2}U_{xxx}+U_{x}U_{xx}^{2}\right)+\left(\frac{\lambda}{5}\right)^{4}U_{x}^{5}, (2.9)

and, in turn again potentialises under

ux=−52​λ​exp⁡(−2​λ5​U)\displaystyle u_{x}=-\frac{5}{2\lambda}\exp\left(-\frac{2\lambda}{5}U\right) (2.10)

in a second-potential Kupershmidt equation,

ut=ux​x​x​x​x−5​ux​x​ux​x​x​xux−15​ux​x​x24​ux+65​ux​x2​ux​x​xux2−135​ux​x416​ux3.\displaystyle u_{t}=u_{xxxxx}-\frac{5u_{xx}u_{xxxx}}{u_{x}}-\frac{15u_{xxx}^{2}}{4u_{x}}+\frac{65u_{xx}^{2}u_{xxx}}{u_{x}^{2}}-\frac{135u_{xx}^{4}}{16u_{x}^{3}}. (2.11)

In addition, the first potential Kupershmidt equation (2.9) also potentialises in

vt=vx​x​x​x​x−5​vx​x​vx​x​x​xvx+5​vx​x2​vx​x​xvx2\displaystyle v_{t}=v_{xxxxx}-5\frac{v_{xx}v_{xxxx}}{v_{x}}+5\frac{v_{xx}^{2}v_{xxx}}{v_{x}^{2}} (2.12)

under

vx=5λ​exp⁡(λ5​U).\displaystyle v_{x}=\frac{5}{\lambda}\exp\left(\frac{\lambda}{5}U\right). (2.13)

A connection between the Kupershmidt equation, (2.7), and the equation (2.11) is given by the differential substitution

K⁡(x,t)=−52​λ​ux​xux,\displaystyle K(x,t)=-\frac{5}{2\lambda}\frac{u_{xx}}{u_{x}}, (2.14)

which is obtained by combining Ux=KU_{x}=K and ux=−5/(2λ)exp(−2U/(5λ)u_{x}=-5/(2\lambda)\exp(-2U/(5\lambda).

Furthermore, we can connect the first potential Kupershmidt equation, (2.9), and the Kaup-Kupershmidt equation

Qt=Qx​x​x​x+μ​Q​Qx​x​x+5​μ2​Qx​Qx​x+μ25​Q2​Qx\displaystyle Q_{t}=Q_{xxxx}+\mu QQ_{xxx}+\frac{5\mu}{2}Q_{x}Q_{xx}+\frac{\mu^{2}}{5}Q^{2}Q_{x} (2.15)

for arbitrary constant μ≠0\mu\neq 0, by the differential substitution (given in [6] for the special case, μ=5\mu=5 and λ=5\lambda=5)

Q=(2​λμ)​Ux​x−(λ5​μ)​Ux2.\displaystyle Q=\left(\frac{2\lambda}{\mu}\right)U_{xx}-\left(\frac{\lambda}{5\mu}\right)U_{x}^{2}. (2.16)

We now focus our attention on equation (2.11). For this equation the most general second-order integrating factors are

Λ1[u]=αux−5/2ux​x,Λ2[u]=α(uux−5/2ux​x−2ux−1/2),\displaystyle\Lambda_{1}[u]=\alpha u_{x}^{-5/2}u_{xx},\qquad\Lambda_{2}[u]=\alpha\left(uu_{x}^{-5/2}u_{xx}-2u_{x}^{-1/2}\right), (2.17)

which leads to two potentialisations in (2.12) with α=−3/4\alpha=-3/4, namely

v1,x=ux−1/2,v2,x=uux−1/2,\displaystyle v_{1,x}=u_{x}^{-1/2},\qquad v_{2,x}=uu_{x}^{-1/2}, (2.18)

respectively. See the Diagram below. Furthermore, the most general second-order integrating factors of equation (2.12) are

Λn[v]=vnvx​xvx2−n2vn−11vx2,n=0,1,2,3,4.\displaystyle\Lambda_{n}[v]=v^{n}\frac{v_{xx}}{v_{x}^{2}}-\frac{n}{2}v^{n-1}\frac{1}{v_{x}^{2}},\quad n=0,1,2,3,4. (2.19)

The integrating factor Λ0\Lambda_{0} and Λ4\Lambda_{4} lead to the potentialisation of equation (2.12) in equation (2.11), namely

u3,x=vx−2,u4,x=v4​vx−2,\displaystyle u_{3,x}=v_{x}^{-2},\qquad u_{4,x}=v^{4}v_{x}^{-2}, (2.20)

respectively. See the Diagram below.

Combining the above potentialisations for the equation (2.11) and the equation (2.12), leads to the following △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformations for these equations:

Proposition 2: The equation (2.11), viz.

ut=ux​x​x​x​x−5​ux​x​ux​x​x​xux−154​ux​x​x2ux+654​ux​x​x​ux​x2ux2−13516​ux​x4ux3\displaystyle u_{t}=u_{xxxxx}-5\frac{u_{xx}u_{xxxx}}{u_{x}}-\frac{15}{4}\frac{u_{xxx}^{2}}{u_{x}}+\frac{65}{4}\frac{u_{xxx}u_{xx}^{2}}{u_{x}^{2}}-\frac{135}{16}\frac{u_{xx}^{4}}{u_{x}^{3}}

admits the following △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformations:

uj+1,x​x=uj+1,x​[uj,x​xuj,x−2​uj,xuj]+4​uj+1,x3/4​[uj1/2uj,x1/4],\displaystyle u_{j+1,xx}=u_{j+1,x}\left[\frac{u_{j,xx}}{u_{j,x}}-2\frac{u_{j,x}}{u_{j}}\right]+4\,u_{j+1,x}^{3/4}\left[\frac{u_{j}^{1/2}}{u_{j,x}^{1/4}}\right], (2.21a)
uj+1,x​x=uj+1,x​[uj,x​xuj,x]+4​uj+1,x3/4​[1uj,x1/4],\displaystyle u_{j+1,xx}=u_{j+1,x}\left[\frac{u_{j,xx}}{u_{j,x}}\right]+4\,u_{j+1,x}^{3/4}\left[\frac{1}{u_{j,x}^{1/4}}\right], (2.21b)

where uju_{j} and uj+1u_{j+1} satisfy (2.11) for all natural numbers jj.

Proposition 3: The equation (2.12), viz.

vt=vx​x​x​x​x−5​vx​x​vx​x​x​xvx+5​vx​x2​vx​x​xvx2,\displaystyle v_{t}=v_{xxxxx}-5\frac{v_{xx}v_{xxxx}}{v_{x}}+5\frac{v_{xx}^{2}v_{xxx}}{v_{x}^{2}},

admits the following △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformations:

vj+1,x​x=vj+1,x​[vj,x​xvj,x]−1vj,x,\displaystyle v_{j+1,xx}=v_{j+1,x}\left[\frac{v_{j,xx}}{v_{j,x}}\right]-\frac{1}{v_{j,x}}, (2.22a)
vj+1,x​x=vj+1,x​[vj,x​xvj,x]+1vj,x,\displaystyle v_{j+1,xx}=v_{j+1,x}\left[\frac{v_{j,xx}}{v_{j,x}}\right]+\frac{1}{v_{j,x}}, (2.22b)
vj+1,x​x=vj+1,x​[vj,x​xvj,x−2​vj,xvj]+vj2vj,x,\displaystyle v_{j+1,xx}=v_{j+1,x}\left[\frac{v_{j,xx}}{v_{j,x}}-2\,\frac{v_{j,x}}{v_{j}}\right]+\frac{v_{j}^{2}}{v_{j,x}}, (2.22c)

where vjv_{j} and vj+1v_{j+1} satisfy (2.12) for all natural numbers jj.

Remark 1: We note that in addition to the transformations given by Proposition 2 and Proposition 3, both (2.11) and (2.12) admit the symmetry transformation

uj+1=−1uj+constant,vj+1=−1vj+constant\displaystyle u_{j+1}=-\frac{1}{u_{j}}+\mbox{constant},\qquad v_{j+1}=-\frac{1}{v_{j}}+\mbox{constant} (2.23)

which are included in the Diagram: combine vx=u1,x−1/2v_{x}=u_{1,x}^{-1/2} with vx=u2u2,x−1/2v_{x}=u_{2}u_{2,x}^{-1/2}, and ux=v1,x−2u_{x}=v_{1,x}^{-2} with ux=v24​v2,x−2u_{x}=v_{2}^{4}v_{2,x}^{-2}, respectively. Note that these relations were also identified by Weiss (see relation (3.37) in [9]).

Remark 2: The △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformations (2.21a) and (2.21b) given in Proposition 2 can be linearised, as those are in the form of first-order Bernoulli equations under the substitution uj+1,x=wj+1u_{j+1,x}=w_{j+1}.

3 Solutions

In the above Diagram it is clear that equation (2.12), viz.

vt=vx​x​x​x​x−5​vx​x​vx​x​x​xvx+5​vx​x2​vx​x​xvx2,\displaystyle v_{t}=v_{xxxxx}-\frac{5v_{xx}v_{xxxx}}{v_{x}}+\frac{5v_{xx}^{2}v_{xxx}}{v_{x}^{2}},

plays a central role in the connection between the Kupershmidt-, the Kaup-Kupershmidt and equation (2.11).

We now find the most general stationary solution for equation (2.12) by calculating the first integrals and the general solution of the ordinary differential equation

vx​x​x​x​x−5​vx​x​vx​x​x​xvx+5​vx​x2​vx​x​xvx2=0.\displaystyle v_{xxxxx}-\frac{5v_{xx}v_{xxxx}}{v_{x}}+\frac{5v_{xx}^{2}v_{xxx}}{v_{x}^{2}}=0. (3.1)

We find that equation (3.1) admits five second-order integrating factors, {Λ0,Λ1,Λ2,Λ3,Λ4}\{\Lambda_{0},\Lambda_{1},\Lambda_{2},\Lambda_{3},\Lambda_{4}\}:

Λn​(x,v,vx,vx​x)=an​vx​xvx2−an′2​1vx2,\displaystyle\Lambda_{n}(x,v,v_{x},v_{xx})=a_{n}\frac{v_{xx}}{v_{x}^{2}}-\frac{a_{n}^{\prime}}{2}\frac{1}{v_{x}^{2}}, (3.2)

where

an​(v)=vnwithn=0,1,2,3,4.\displaystyle a_{n}(v)=v^{n}\qquad\mbox{with}\quad n=0,1,2,3,4.

Here the primes denote derivatives with respect to vv. The corresponding five first integrals are then

In=(an​vx​xvx4−12​an′vx2)​vx​x​x​x−12​an​vx​x​x2vx4+(12​an′​vx​xvx3−an​vx​x2vx5+12​an′′vx)​vx​x​x\displaystyle I_{n}=\left(a_{n}\frac{v_{xx}}{v_{x}^{4}}-\frac{1}{2}\frac{a_{n}^{\prime}}{v_{x}^{2}}\right)v_{xxxx}-\frac{1}{2}a_{n}\frac{v_{xxx}^{2}}{v_{x}^{4}}+\left(\frac{1}{2}a_{n}^{\prime}\frac{v_{xx}}{v_{x}^{3}}-a_{n}\frac{v_{xx}^{2}}{v_{x}^{5}}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{a_{n}^{\prime\prime}}{v_{x}}\right)v_{xxx}
−12​an′′′​vx​x+14​an(4)​vx2,n=0,1,2,3,4.\displaystyle\qquad-\frac{1}{2}a_{n}^{\prime\prime\prime}v_{xx}+\frac{1}{4}a_{n}^{(4)}v_{x}^{2},\qquad n=0,1,2,3,4.

Combining I0,I1,I2,I3I_{0},\ I_{1},\ I_{2},\ I_{3} and I4I_{4}, we obtain

vx=(I0​v4−4​I1​v3+6​I2​v2−4​I3​v+I4)1/2,\displaystyle v_{x}=\left(I_{0}v^{4}-4I_{1}v^{3}+6I_{2}v^{2}-4I_{3}v+I_{4}\right)^{1/2},

with the condition

I0​I4−4​I1​I3+3​I22=0.\displaystyle I_{0}I_{4}-4I_{1}I_{3}+3I_{2}^{2}=0.

So the general solution of (3.1) is given by the quadrature

∫(I0v4−4I1v3+6I2v2−4I3v+I4)−1/2dv=x+C,\displaystyle\int\left(I_{0}v^{4}-4I_{1}v^{3}+6I_{2}v^{2}-4I_{3}v+I_{4}\right)^{-1/2}dv=x+C, (3.3)

where CC is a constant of integration. Since the quadrature (3.3) contains five independent free constants, it represents the most general stationary solution of (2.12). This solution can now be used to generate nonstationary solutions for (2.12) by the △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformations of Proposition 3 and, by applying the transformations in the above Diagram, solutions of (2.11) can be constructed. Then by Proposition 1, the so constructed solutions of (2.11) lead to solutions of the Kaup-Kupershmidt equation, as well as solutions of the Kupershmidt equation by the differential substitution (2.14).

For example, by (3.3) with I0=I1=I2=I4=C=0I_{0}=I_{1}=I_{2}=I_{4}=C=0 and I3=−2I_{3}=-2 we obtain the solution

v⁡(x,t)=2​x2\displaystyle v(x,t)=2x^{2}

for (2.12) and hence the solution

u⁡(x,t)=16​x\displaystyle u(x,t)=16x

for (2.11). Applying now, for example, the △\bigtriangleup-auto-Bäcklund transformation (2.21a) leads to the solution

u⁡(x,t)=17​x7−45​c1​x5+2​c12​x3−4​c13​x−c14​x−1−576​c1​t+c2,\displaystyle u(x,t)=\frac{1}{7}x^{7}-\frac{4}{5}c_{1}x^{5}+2c_{1}^{2}x^{3}-4c_{1}^{3}x-c_{1}^{4}x^{-1}-576c_{1}t+c_{2},

where c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} are arbitrary constants. Appplying again (2.21a), setting c1=c2=0c_{1}=c_{2}=0 for simplicity, we obtain the following solution for (2.11):

u⁡(x,t)=154⋅7⋅91​x13+3653⋅7​x8​t+27⋅3452​x3​t2−212⋅38⋅7​x−7​t4−210⋅36⋅75​x−2​t3.\displaystyle u(x,t)=\frac{1}{5^{4}\cdot 7\cdot 91}x^{13}+\frac{36}{5^{3}\cdot 7}x^{8}t+\frac{2^{7}\cdot 3^{4}}{5^{2}}x^{3}t^{2}-2^{12}\cdot 3^{8}\cdot 7x^{-7}t^{4}-\frac{2^{10}\cdot 3^{6}\cdot 7}{5}x^{-2}t^{3}.

Proposition 1 can now be applied with the above solutions of (2.11) (put u⁡(x,t)≡B⁡(x,t)u(x,t)\equiv B(x,t) in (1.2) and (1.3)) to gain solutions for the Kaup-Kupershmidt equation (1.1). Furthermore, solutions of the Kupershmidt equation, (2.7), are then given by the differential substitution (2.14).
